plan.topic: How labs that study plague keep it contained: biosafety levels (BSL-3), airflow, PPE, and standard steps after a possible lab exposure
plan.angle: Plague Labs: How Do Scientists Keep Dangerous Bacteria Contained? A general biosafety explainer from CDC/NIH BMBL (6th ed.) and WHO's Laboratory Biosafety Manual (4th ed.). What biosafety levels mean, and how BMBL scales Y. pestis work: BSL-2 practices and facilities for most clinical-sample and culture work, BSL-3 for aerosol-generating, large-scale or some animal work. Say clearly that this is the US/WHO framework and that countries, including Russia, use their own classification systems. Cover inward airflow and HEPA exhaust, biosafety cabinets, respirators and PPE, training and incident reporting. Then the standard post-exposure steps: report straight away, medical review, monitoring through the incubation window, and preventive antibiotics only when clinicians decide they're needed (no self-treatment). Dated status box: 'As of Oct 8, 2026: plague was suspected in media reports and has not been officially confirmed. Rospotrebnadzor reported that nearly 5,000 lab tests found no dangerous pathogens, that medical monitoring was completed for over 90% of contacts, and that quarantine measures were lifted in Irkutsk oblast. WHO says it does not know what caused the Oct 2 death and has asked Russia for more information. Not confirmed isn't ruled out.' Credit any incident detail to a named outlet ('reported by Reuters/AP'). No leak, bioweapon or blame framing, and don't name or show the worker. Close with 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.' Thumbnail: lab scene with a biosafety cabinet.
plan.working_title: Plague Labs: How Do Scientists Keep Dangerous Bacteria Contained?
plan.why: The radar puts this at the emerging stage (momentum 70, low competition, seen in 3 snapshots). NYT, Defector and The Conversation are covering the institute, but almost no explainer covers lab safety itself. It has 8–15 minutes of guideline-backed depth and is a pillar we haven't covered yet. | fact-check: Lab safety is a good, calm pillar, but two parts of the angle are wrong. (1) Scope: in the CDC/NIH BMBL agent summary for Yersinia pestis, BSL-2 practices, containment equipment and facilities are recommended for most work with clinical materials and cultures. BSL-3 is for work with a high potential for aerosol or droplet production, large-scale production, and some infected-animal work. So 'usually done at BSL-3' overstates it. (2) Status box: 'contact observation has ended' is stronger than the source. Rospotrebnadzor said medical monitoring was completed for 'over 90%' of contacts (reported Oct 8). The test figure was reported as 'nearly 5,000', not 'about 5,000'. The claim that 'no plague was recorded' came from Russian authorities via WHO, so credit it to them. Also: BSL-1 to BSL-4 is the US/WHO framework, and Russia classifies pathogens under its own system. Don't say or imply that the Irkutsk institute uses the BMBL BSL scheme. Leave out the governor's 'patient was vaccinated' claim, or credit it to him by name as a reported statement, with no inference. 'Lab-acquired plague is rare' needs a citable source (e.g. BMBL's note on reported laboratory-acquired infections). If you can't find one, drop it. Re-check the status at publish time.

package.description:
Most plague lab work isn't done in space-suit labs. Under the US BMBL guide (CDC/NIH), BSL-2 is recommended for most work with plague clinical samples and cultures; BSL-3 for work with high droplet/aerosol potential, large-scale production or high concentrations. A lab's risk assessment can call for more. BSL-3 labs add inward airflow, non-recirculated exhaust, HEPA-filtered biosafety cabinets, protective gear and training.

As of Oct 8, 2026: plague was suspected in media reports after a lab worker's death in Irkutsk oblast, Russia. It has not been officially confirmed. Rospotrebnadzor says the cause was pneumonia of unknown etiology, and on Oct 8 said about 5,000 lab tests found no dangerous pathogens and its anti-epidemic measures were finished. WHO (Oct 6-7) has asked Russia for information. Not confirmed isn't ruled out.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Possible exposure (like close contact with someone who has pneumonic plague) plus fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain? Contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.

Sources:
1. BMBL, 6th Ed. (CDC/NIH): https://www.cdc.gov/labs/bmbl/index.html
2. WHO plague fact sheet: https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/plague
3. CDC MMWR 2021, plague treatment and prophylaxis: https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/70/rr/rr7003a1.htm
4. Kyiv Independent (Oct 8, 2026): https://kyivindependent.com/russia-lifts-quarantine-in-irkutsk-region-where-lab-worker-allegedly-died-of-plague/

script.working_title: Plague Labs: How Do Scientists Keep Dangerous Bacteria Contained?
script.hook_pattern: Counterintuitive claim, followed by an open loop ("one safety step that everything else depends on isn't a machine"), paid off in the final chapter

scenes.narration: Most lab work with plague bacteria doesn't happen in the space-suit labs you see in movies. That's not a loophole. It's the design.

visual.stock_query: scientist at biosafety cabinet bright lab

scenes.retention_device: Counterintuitive cold open that breaks the movie stereotype

scenes.narration: Under the main US lab safety guide, biosafety level 2 practices, equipment and facilities are recommended for most work with clinical samples and cultures of Yersinia pestis, the bacterium behind plague. The stricter level 3 is recommended for the riskiest tasks.

visual.myth: All plague lab work needs maximum security
visual.fact: BMBL: BSL-2 for most sample and culture work, BSL-3 for aerosol-risk tasks

scenes.retention_device: Proof point that backs the hook straight away

scenes.narration: Why? Because in a lab, the big worry isn't bacteria sitting quietly in a dish. It's what happens if they get into the air.

visual.stock_query: petri dish with tiny droplets floating

scenes.narration: In the next few minutes, you'll see what those levels mean, how a lab pulls air inward so germs can't drift out, and the box that shields a scientist's lungs.
scenes.retention_device: Promise of what the viewer gets

scenes.narration: And stay to the end, because one safety step that everything else depends on isn't a machine at all. It's something a person does in the first few minutes.
scenes.retention_device: Main open loop, paid off in the final chapter

scenes.narration: Why now? As of October 8, 2026, plague was suspected in media reports after a death in Irkutsk oblast, Russia, and has not been officially confirmed. Russian authorities say the cause is unknown. We'll go through what's been said later.
scenes.retention_device: Topical stakes plus a second open loop (the status chapter)

scenes.narration: One note up front: this is a general explainer of the US and WHO framework. Other countries can use their own national rules, so this doesn't describe how any specific Russian lab works.

visual.stock_query: rulebooks with different covers on shelf

scenes.retention_device: Sets the scope clearly so viewers trust what follows

scenes.narration: First, the levels. The US guide is called Biosafety in Microbiological and Biomedical Laboratories, or BMBL. It's published by CDC and the National Institutes of Health, and it's on its 6th edition.

visual.stock_query: thick lab safety manual on desk

scenes.retention_device: Chapter reset with a named, credible source

scenes.narration: It lays out 4 biosafety levels. Think of them like layers of rain gear: the worse the weather, the more layers you put on.

Level 1 is for microbes not known to consistently cause disease in healthy adults. Level 2 covers moderate hazards, like hepatitis B or Salmonella, where the main risks are cuts, splashes and swallowing.

visual.stock_query: lab bench with gloves and goggles

scenes.narration: Level 3 is for germs that can cause serious or potentially lethal disease when breathed in, like the bacterium that causes tuberculosis.
Level 4 is the space-suit level, for dangerous and exotic agents like Ebola virus, with a high risk of life-threatening infection and often no vaccine or treatment.
scenes.retention_device: Pays off the space-suit image from the hook

scenes.narration: But here's the twist. The World Health Organization's latest Laboratory Biosafety Manual, the 4th edition from 2020, moved away from leaning on those numbered levels.
Instead, WHO says every lab should start with a risk assessment. What exactly are you doing, with which germ, and how could it get out? Then you choose controls to match.

visual.stock_query: scientist with clipboard and question marks

scenes.narration: WHO sorts those controls into 3 tiers: core requirements for most lab work, heightened control measures for higher risk, and maximum containment measures for the very highest.
So the same germ can need different precautions depending on the task. And plague is a perfect example.

visual.stock_query: one test tube two lab setups

scenes.narration: BMBL includes a summary written specifically for Yersinia pestis. It recommends level 2 practices, containment equipment and facilities for most work with clinical samples and cultures.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter reset with a specific answer

scenes.narration: Level 3 is recommended for work with a high potential to create droplets or aerosols, and for large-scale production or high concentrations of the bacteria. And a lab's own risk assessment can call for stricter precautions.

visual.stock_query: lab tasks icons in a row

scenes.narration: Why the split? Gently transferring a sample is very different from spinning, shaking or mixing a big culture, steps that can throw tiny droplets into the air.
And air is the route that matters. According to CDC, pneumonic plague, the lung form, is the form that can spread between people, through respiratory droplets during close contact.

visual.stock_query: two people close with droplet icons

scenes.retention_device: Links the lab to the disease the news is about

scenes.narration: BMBL also notes that laboratory-acquired plague infections have been reported. So staff are told to take special care not to create aerosols.
scenes.retention_device: Shows the stakes are real, setting up later chapters

scenes.narration: So what does a level 3 lab actually look like inside? Let's walk up to the door.
scenes.retention_device: Question to the viewer leading into the next chapter

scenes.narration: First, you can't just wander in. Under BMBL, access to a level 3 lab is restricted, and it's separated from parts of the building with open traffic.
You go through 2 self-closing doors, often with a small changing room in between. It's a buffer between the lab and the hallway.

visual.stat_label: Self-closing doors into a BSL-3 lab

scenes.narration: Now the clever part: the air. A level 3 lab must keep air flowing in from clean areas toward areas that might be contaminated.

visual.stock_query: arrows of air flowing into lab

scenes.narration: Picture a gentle, steady breeze blowing from the hallway into the room. If a droplet ever escaped a container, that breeze carries it deeper into the lab, not out the door.

visual.stock_query: breeze pushing droplet away from door

scenes.narration: Staff must be able to check that airflow, with a monitor at the entrance. And the system must be designed so that under failure conditions, the airflow will not be reversed.
Where does the air go? Never back into the rest of the building. BMBL says lab exhaust must not recirculate. It's sent away from people and air intakes, or it's HEPA-filtered.
The room is built to be cleaned: sealed surfaces, sealed windows, and a hands-free sink near the exit.

visual.stock_query: clean sealed lab room with sink

scenes.narration: And waste doesn't leave untreated. BMBL says a way to decontaminate all lab waste should be on hand, ideally inside the lab, such as an autoclave, which is essentially a high-pressure steam oven.
But here's what surprises most people. The room isn't the main barrier. Under BMBL, the primary barrier at level 3 is about the size of a desk.
It's called a biological safety cabinet. At level 3, BMBL says all handling of infectious material happens inside one, or inside another physical containment device.
The most common kind, Class II, has an open front where the scientist's arms go in. That gap isn't sealed shut. It's guarded by air.
Air is pulled in through the front, away from the worker. Filtered air flows down over the work, protecting the sample. And air leaving the cabinet is filtered too.
One box, 3 jobs: protect the person, protect the sample, protect the room.
Those filters are HEPA filters, rated to trap at least 99.97% of particles 0.3 microns across, about the size that's hardest to catch. Larger and smaller particles are trapped even more efficiently.
For the highest-risk work there's Class III: a fully sealed box. Scientists work through heavy gloves attached to the front and never reach inside directly.
And the everyday rules stay strict. BMBL's wording is blunt: 'Mouth pipetting is prohibited.' No eating, drinking or applying cosmetics in the lab, and sharp items get extra care.

visual.stock_query: no food no drink lab sign

scenes.retention_device: Real quote breaks up the pattern

scenes.narration: Machines only get you so far, though. The next layer is the one you can see: what the scientist wears.
scenes.retention_device: Transition hook into the next chapter

scenes.narration: At level 3, BMBL calls for protective clothing with a solid front, like wrap-around gowns or coveralls, that stays in the lab.
Gloves, with 2 pairs when appropriate. Eye and face protection. And respiratory protection, such as a fitted respirator, chosen based on the lab's risk assessment.
A respirator only works if it seals to your face. In the US, OSHA requires workers who must wear tight-fitting respirators to be fit tested and trained.
scenes.on_screen_text: A seal, not just a mask

scenes.narration: Then there's training. Before working with level 3 agents, staff must show they're proficient in the lab's practices, not just read the manual.
scenes.on_screen_text: Show it, don't just read it

scenes.narration: BMBL also calls for medical surveillance, meaning health checks linked to the work, and offering vaccines where appropriate ones exist.
In the US there's a legal layer too. Yersinia pestis is a Tier 1 select agent, the highest-security category under the Federal Select Agent Program.

visual.stat_label: US select agent category for plague bacteria

scenes.narration: Labs must register to have it, and people need a security risk assessment before they get access.
All of this aims to prevent accidents. But no system assumes it's perfect. So what happens if someone thinks they might have been exposed?
scenes.retention_device: Question cliffhanger before the chapter change

scenes.narration: BMBL is clear. Incidents that could cause exposure must be evaluated immediately, reported to the lab supervisor, and followed by medical evaluation, with records kept.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter reset with a clear rule

scenes.narration: Think of it as 4 steps: report, review, monitor, and treat only if clinicians decide it's needed.
Step 1 is reporting immediately. Not after the experiment. Not tomorrow. WHO's manual puts a strong safety culture, where incidents get reported, at the heart of lab biosafety.
scenes.retention_device: Short punchy sentences, hinting at the main payoff

scenes.narration: Step 2 is a medical review. A clinician looks at what happened: which strain, which procedure, and whether there was a spill, a splash or a possible aerosol.
Step 3 is monitoring. WHO says plague's incubation period is 1 to 7 days, and for pneumonic plague it can be as short as 24 hours. So people are watched through that window.

Step 4 is preventive antibiotics, only when clinicians decide they're needed. CDC's 2021 guidance lists lab workers with an accidental exposure to infectious material among the people who may be offered a short preventive course.
That's a medical decision made case by case by clinicians and health authorities. It's never self-treatment.

visual.myth: Exposed? Take antibiotics on your own
visual.fact: Clinicians and health authorities decide case by case

scenes.narration: Why does speed matter so much? Because plague can be treated with commonly available antibiotics, and CDC and WHO both stress that early treatment is key.
And there's a real case that shows why that first step, speaking up, matters.
In 2009, a researcher in Chicago died of plague after working with a weakened lab strain of Yersinia pestis.
CDC investigators reported that he had an undiagnosed condition called hereditary hemochromatosis, which makes iron build up in the body.
That turned out to matter. The weakened strain had a defect in how it gathers iron, which plague bacteria need to cause disease. Investigators suggested his extra iron may have helped it grow.

Investigators couldn't say exactly how he was exposed. But the lesson is practical: weakened doesn't automatically mean harmless, and if you work with these bacteria and get sick, tell your doctor about your work right away.
scenes.retention_device: Practical lesson that sets up the main payoff

scenes.narration: Which brings us back to the news, and what's actually been said so far.
scenes.retention_device: Pays off the status loop from the hook

scenes.narration: AP and other outlets reported that a laboratory worker in Irkutsk oblast, Russia, died on October 2 after a severe pneumonia, and that plague was suspected. Out of respect, we're not naming or showing her.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter reset with clearly attributed facts

scenes.narration: Here's the status as of October 8, 2026, the date of the latest official statements we found. Plague was suspected in media reports. Russia's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, says the cause was pneumonia of unknown etiology, and that tests on her samples found no microbes linked to her work. Plague has not been officially confirmed.
On October 8, Rospotrebnadzor said about 5,000 lab tests found no dangerous pathogens. Earlier, it said daily testing of contacts had found only 2 cases of COVID-19 and 2 of rhinovirus.

visual.stat_label: Lab tests, no dangerous pathogens (Rospotrebnadzor, Oct 8)

scenes.narration: On October 8, Rospotrebnadzor said it had finished its anti-epidemic measures, including medical observation of more than 90% of contacts, and said there were no epidemic risks for the population of the Irkutsk region. The Kyiv Independent reports the quarantine has been lifted.

visual.stat_label: Contacts under medical observation, per Rospotrebnadzor (Oct 8)

scenes.retention_device: Second stat in a row keeps momentum

scenes.narration: WHO says it's still asking questions. On October 6, Director-General Tedros said WHO had asked Russia for information, and on October 7 WHO's Maria Van Kerkhove said, 'We don't understand how she was infected.'

visual.quote: We don't understand how she was infected.
visual.attribution: Maria Van Kerkhove, WHO, October 7, 2026 (reported by AP)
visual.stock_query: globe on desk with question mark

scenes.retention_device: Credits each statement to the person and date that made it

scenes.narration: So hold 2 ideas at once. Not confirmed isn't the same as ruled out. And this can change quickly, so check the latest official update.

visual.fact: Not confirmed isn't ruled out. Check official updates.

scenes.retention_device: Myth correction plus an instruction to the viewer

scenes.narration: And remember, the biosafety levels in this video are the US and WHO framework. Other countries can use their own national rules, so these labels may not map neatly onto Russian labs.
scenes.retention_device: Repeats the scope so nobody misreads it

scenes.narration: So, the step everything else depends on? It isn't the cabinet or the airflow. It's a person reporting a possible exposure right away, which BMBL requires immediately.
Every other layer, the medical review, the monitoring, and preventive antibiotics when clinicians decide they're needed, can only start once someone speaks up.

Quick recap. Precautions match the task. Under BMBL, most plague sample and culture work is level 2, and aerosol-risk or large-scale work is level 3, and a risk assessment can call for more. Air flows inward. Cabinets and HEPA filters do the heavy lifting. And fast reporting means fast care.

For everyone else: if you've had a possible exposure, like close contact with someone who has pneumonic plague, and you develop fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain, contact a doctor or local health authority urgently.
If you're worried, talk to a health professional.
Next, we're breaking down pneumonic plague symptoms and exactly when CDC says to get urgent care. Subscribe so it's ready when you need it.
scenes.retention_device: CTA tied to the next video's specific benefit

factcheck.summary: The science in this long-form script holds up well. I verified the BMBL framing (BSL-2 for most Yersinia pestis clinical sample/culture work, BSL-3 for high-aerosol-potential and large-scale/high-concentration work), the WHO 4th-edition risk-assessment approach with its three tiers, WHO's 1–7 day incubation with pneumonic onset as short as 24 hours, the HEPA 99.97% at 0.3 µm specification, Y. pestis as a Tier 1 select agent, OSHA fit-testing, the MMWR 2021 statement that post-exposure prophylaxis "can be considered for laboratory workers accidentally exposed to infectious materials," and every detail of the 2011 MMWR Chicago 2009 case (attenuated pgm-negative KIM D27 strain, C282Y-homozygous hereditary hemochromatosis, iron-acquisition defect, undetermined exposure route). Safety framing is strong: no self-treatment, prophylaxis consistently gated behind clinicians, urgent-care red flags present, the disclaimer line present, the deceased treated with respect, no bioweapon or cover-up speculation, and an explicit scope caveat that this is the US/WHO framework and not a description of any Russian lab. The problems are all in the news chapter's attribution and dating, plus source-list hygiene. Scene s64 dates the "about 5,000 lab tests" figure to Rospotrebnadzor on October 8, but The Moscow Times carries that figure without a date and The Kyiv Independent attributes "nearly 5,000 laboratory tests" to Irkutsk governor Igor Kobzev — this is exactly the mis-crediting pattern that caused prior holds. s65 needs the Kyiv Independent's own verification caveat. s06 omits that Rospotrebnadzor has said no plague was detected, which the viewer only learns 57 scenes later. The BMBL source year needs a last-reviewed date (the CDC page now shows March 18, 2026), the AP/ABC URL uses a non-canonical domain, and one listed source is never cited. Fix these and it's publishable; also re-check the official status at publish time, since the script's status line is dated one day before today.

issues.claim: "On October 8, Rospotrebnadzor said about 5,000 lab tests found no dangerous pathogens." On-screen stat label: "Lab tests, no dangerous pathogens (Rospotrebnadzor, Oct 8)".
issues.problem: The attribution and the date both go beyond the cited sources. The Moscow Times reports the ~5,000-test figure as a Rospotrebnadzor statement but gives no date for it; The Kyiv Independent attributes "nearly 5,000 laboratory tests" to Irkutsk governor Igor Kobzev, not to Rospotrebnadzor. Crediting a figure to the wrong body and stamping an unsupported date on it is the same error that has triggered previous holds.
issues.fix: Replace the narration with: "Around the same time, Irkutsk governor Igor Kobzev said nearly 5,000 laboratory tests had found no dangerous pathogens, as reported by The Kyiv Independent. Earlier, Rospotrebnadzor said daily testing of contacts had found only 2 cases of COVID-19 and 2 of rhinovirus, as reported by AP." Change the stat label to "Nearly 5,000 lab tests, no dangerous pathogens (Gov. Kobzev, per The Kyiv Independent)" and add kyiv_independent to this scene's source_ids.

issues.claim: "The Kyiv Independent reports the quarantine has been lifted."
issues.problem: Correctly attributed, but the Kyiv Independent explicitly notes it could not independently verify some of the official claims in this story. Dropping that caveat presents contested official statements as settled.
issues.fix: Append to the narration: "The Kyiv Independent notes it could not independently verify all of those official claims."

issues.claim: "plague was suspected in media reports after a death in Irkutsk oblast, Russia, and has not been officially confirmed. Russian authorities say the cause is unknown."
issues.problem: Incomplete at the point where most viewers form their impression. Rospotrebnadzor has gone further than "unknown": it has said no plague was detected in the researcher or her contacts and that testing found no microorganisms associated with her work. Holding that back until s63 lets the opening read as more suggestive of plague than the record supports.
issues.fix: Replace the last sentence with: "Russia's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, says the cause was pneumonia of unknown etiology and that no plague was detected. WHO has asked Russia for more information. We'll go through what each body has said later."

issues.claim: "Here's the status as of October 8, 2026, the date of the latest official statements we found."
issues.problem: The status line is already one day old relative to today (October 9, 2026), and this story has been moving daily. Nothing is wrong in the line as written, but it will be stale or wrong if the piece publishes later than scripted.
issues.fix: Keep the dated wording but add a standing instruction in the production notes: re-check WHO, Rospotrebnadzor and CDC at publish time and update the date and the status sentence in s06, s63 and the on-screen text if anything has changed. Add after the first sentence: "Check the latest official update before you act on anything here."

issues.claim: BMBL 6th Edition listed with year "2020" and URL https://www.cdc.gov/labs/bmbl/index.html
issues.problem: The URL is a living landing page, not a dated document. The CDC page currently shows a March 18, 2026 update stamp, and the page itself does not state 2020. Our source-list rule requires a last-reviewed date on living pages.
issues.fix: Change the source entry to: title "Biosafety in Microbiological and Biomedical Laboratories (BMBL), 6th Edition", year "2020 (CDC page last updated 18 March 2026)", and keep the same URL.

issues.problem: Non-canonical domain. ABC News wire stories live at abcnews.go.com; abcnews.com is a redirect host, which risks a dead link in the description and pinned comment.
No scene cites newsnation_who, and the URL is an AMP variant. An uncited source in the list invites the packaging agent to quote something the script never verified.
issues.fix: Delete the newsnation_who entry from the source list.

issues.claim: "Those filters are HEPA filters, rated to trap at least 99.97% of particles 0.3 microns across... Larger and smaller particles are trapped even more efficiently." Source id: bmbl only.
issues.problem: The numbers are correct, but the 99.97%-at-0.3-µm rating and the most-penetrating-particle-size point are filter-standard facts, not something the BMBL Y. pestis or BSL-3 sections state in those terms. Single-sourcing them to BMBL repeats the "source tag doesn't say the line" pattern.
issues.fix: Change the narration to: "Those are HEPA filters. By definition, a HEPA filter traps at least 99.97% of particles 0.3 microns across, about the size that's hardest to catch, and it catches larger and smaller particles even more efficiently." Add the DOE/NIOSH HEPA definition as a source, or drop the final sentence and keep only "at least 99.97% at 0.3 microns".

issues.claim: "CDC's 2021 guidance lists lab workers with an accidental exposure to infectious material among the people who may be offered a short preventive course."
issues.problem: Slightly stronger than the source's verb. MMWR 2021;70(RR-3) says prophylaxis "can be considered for laboratory workers accidentally exposed to infectious materials" — considered, not offered.
issues.fix: Replace with: "CDC's 2021 guidance says preventive antibiotics can be considered for laboratory workers accidentally exposed to infectious materials, as a 7-day course."

thumbnail.reasoning: Candidate #1 ("WHICH IS REAL?", versus layout) has the clearest single focal contrast — two human characters labeled Movies vs Real Lab with red X / green check — which creates an immediate, resolvable curiosity gap tied directly to the video's promise (what BSL-3 labs actually look like vs movie depictions). It also matches the only proven high-performer in our own data: the versus thumbnail layout hit 178 views, our best long-form result, while reaction layouts with lone mascot icons scored much lower (12-15) and our craft notes warn against lone-icon/sparse frames, which #0 and #2 both lean toward (a filing-cabinet-like mascot that doesn't clearly represent a lab). All three are legible at phone size, but #1's text and color-coded labels remain clearly readable even at the smallest size, and its two-character layout gives a stronger, more human focal point than the ambiguous cabinet mascot in #0 and #2. Nothing here is misleading relative to the title, which promises an explanation of real BSL-3 containment design."}

issues.problem: The description is cut off: the source URL is incomplete, so the link is broken and the last line is unfinished. The text is at or over the 1,500-character limit.
issues.fix:
Replace the whole description with this text (about 1,420 characters):

Most plague lab work isn't done in space-suit labs. Under the US BMBL guide (CDC/NIH), BSL-2 is recommended for most work with plague clinical samples and cultures; BSL-3 for work with high droplet/aerosol potential, large-scale production or high concentrations. A lab's risk assessment can call for more.

As of Oct 8, 2026: plague was suspected in media reports after a lab worker's death in Irkutsk oblast, Russia, and has not been officially confirmed. Rospotrebnadzor says the cause was pneumonia of unknown etiology; on Oct 8 it said about 5,000 lab tests found no dangerous pathogens and its anti-epidemic measures were finished. On Oct 6, WHO said it had asked Russia for information. Not confirmed isn't ruled out.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Possible exposure (like close contact with someone who has pneumonic plague) plus fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain? Contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.

Sources:
1. BMBL 6th Ed. (CDC/NIH): https://www.cdc.gov/labs/bmbl/index.html
2. WHO plague fact sheet: https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/plague
3. CDC MMWR 2021, plague prophylaxis: https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/70/rr/rr7003a1.htm
4. Kyiv Independent, Oct 8, 2026: https://kyivindependent.com/russia-lifts-quarantine-in-irkutsk-region-where-lab-worker-allegedly-died-of-plague/
